subject: history
summary: Al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya ('The Beginning and the End') is the monumental historical encyclopedia by Imam Ismail ibn Kathir al-Dimashqi (d. 774 AH / 1373 CE), covering history from the creation of the universe through the end times. It is one of the most widely read classical Islamic histories and the primary source for the Prophetic biography and the history of the early Islamic community.
overview:
Al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya ('The Beginning and the End') by Imam Isma'il ibn Kathir al-Dimashqi (700–774 AH / 1301–1373 CE) is the most comprehensive Islamic historical encyclopedia produced in the classical period. Ibn Kathir was a student of Ibn Taymiyyah and a leading scholar of Shafi'i fiqh, hadith, and tafsir in fourteenth-century Damascus. His historical work is inseparable from his better-known Tafsir al-Qur'an al-Azim — both draw on the same encyclopedic hadith knowledge.

The work begins with the primordial creation: the Throne, the Pen, the heavens and earth, the angels, and the creation of Adam عليه السلام. It proceeds through the stories of all the prophets mentioned in the Quran, drawing extensively on Quranic verses, authenticated hadith, and — with careful attribution and editorial caution — the Isra'iliyyat (narrations of Israelite origin). Ibn Kathir consistently flags weak or rejected narrations, making his methodology more rigorous than many earlier Islamic historians.

The Seerah section (biography of the Prophet ﷺ) occupies a substantial portion and is one of the most detailed pre-modern treatments. Ibn Kathir drew on Ibn Hisham's Seerah, the Maghazi of al-Waqidi (with critical evaluation), Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, and dozens of other sources. The work then covers the Rightly-Guided Caliphs (khulafa rashidun), the Umayyad and Abbasid periods, and extends into his own era.

The final section, al-Nihaya ('The End'), addresses eschatology: the signs of the Day of Judgment, the coming of al-Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa عليه السلام, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog), the events of the Barzakh, the resurrection, the Bridge (Sirat), the intercession (shafa'ah), Paradise, and Hell. This section is among the most detailed classical treatments of Islamic eschatology and is cited extensively in academic and popular Islamic literature on the subject.

The standard printed edition runs to twenty-one volumes (Dar Ihya' al-Turath al-Arabi, Beirut). English translations of the Seerah portion and the eschatological volume are available. The work shaped later Islamic historiography profoundly and is indispensable for any study of Islamic history from a primary-source perspective.
structure: 21 volumes; organized chronologically from creation through the author's era, with final eschatological volume

translations.translator: Various (partial — Seerah and eschatology volumes most commonly translated)
